summary: Matthew 17 centers on the Transfiguration and its aftermath. Six days after foretelling His suffering, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John "up into an high mountain apart" and is "transfigured before them": His face "did shine as the sun," His raiment "white as the light." Moses and Elijah appear talking with Him. Peter, wishing to prolong the moment, offers to build three tabernacles, but a "bright cloud" overshadows them and a voice declares, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him." The disciples fall on their faces in fear until Jesus touches them: "Arise, and be not afraid." Coming down, He charges them to tell the vision to no one "until the Son of man be risen again from the dead," and explains that Elijah "is come already" in one they did not recognize—understood to be John the Baptist. At the foot of the mountain a father kneels for his "lunatick" son whom the disciples could not cure. Jesus rebukes the demon and heals the boy "from that very hour," then tells the disciples their failure was "because of your unbelief": faith "as a grain of mustard seed" can move mountains, and "this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting." He again foretells that the Son of man "shall be betrayed... and they shall kill him, and the third day he shall be raised," leaving them "exceeding sorry." Finally, at Capernaum, when the temple-tax collectors ask whether Jesus pays tribute, He teaches Peter that "the children" are free, yet, "lest we should offend them," sends him to find a coin in a fish's mouth to pay for them both.
takeaways: The Transfiguration reveals Jesus' hidden divine glory to three chosen witnesses, confirming His identity just after He first foretold His death.
The Father's voice—"This is my beloved Son... hear ye him"—commands obedient listening to Jesus, who stands above Moses (the Law) and Elijah (the Prophets).
Jesus links the glory of the mountain to the coming cross and resurrection, forbidding the disciples to speak of the vision "until the Son of man be risen again from the dead."
The disciples' failure to heal the boy is traced to "unbelief"; even faith "as a grain of mustard seed" is powerful, and some deliverance comes only "by prayer and fasting."
In the temple-tax episode Jesus both asserts His freedom as the Son and voluntarily accommodates others "lest we should offend them," providing the coin through a quiet miracle.

crossRefs.label: Exodus 24:15-18 — Moses on the mountain, the cloud, and the glory of the LORD
crossRefs.why: Moses ascends the mountain, a cloud covers it, and the glory of the LORD appears; the Transfiguration deliberately echoes this scene, now with Jesus at the center and Moses himself present, casting Jesus as the greater revealer of God's glory.

crossRefs.label: Malachi 4:5-6 — "I will send you Elijah the prophet" before the great day of the LORD
crossRefs.why: The disciples' question about Elijah's coming rests on Malachi's promise; Jesus interprets it as fulfilled in John the Baptist, showing how the prophetic expectation is met and pointing forward to His own suffering.

crossRefs.label: 2 Peter 1:16-18 — an eyewitness of "his majesty" and the voice on the "holy mount"
crossRefs.why: Peter recalls the Transfiguration as firsthand testimony to Jesus' majesty and the Father's voice, confirming the historical claim of Matthew's account and its role as a foretaste of Christ's glory.

crossRefs.label: Daniel 7:9-14 — the Ancient of Days whose garment is "white as snow" and the Son of man
crossRefs.why: Daniel's vision of dazzling white and of "the Son of man" coming in glory stands behind the shining raiment and the title Jesus uses for Himself, framing the Transfiguration as a glimpse of the glory that belongs to the heavenly Son of man.

interpretationNotes.claim: The Catholic tradition reads the Transfiguration as a foretaste of Christ's Resurrection and of the glory promised to His body, the Church. Coming immediately after the first Passion prediction, the mountain vision confirms Peter's confession and strengthens the disciples for the scandal of the cross; the shining of Jesus' face and the Father's testimony disclose His divinity, while the event anticipates the glorification of the faithful in the resurrection of the body.

counterpoint.summary: Protestant interpreters broadly agree that the Transfiguration reveals Jesus' divine glory, confirms the Father's approval, and prepares the disciples for the cross, and many likewise see it as a preview of resurrection glory. They tend, however, to emphasize the command "hear ye him" as establishing Christ's supremacy over Moses and Elijah—the Law and the Prophets now fulfilled and superseded in the Son—more than any developed sacramental theology of a "second regeneration." Both traditions affirm the event discloses Jesus' divinity and points to the glory of resurrection; they differ mainly in how much liturgical and sacramental weight they draw from it.
